newsitem.title: GERMANY: German prosecutors press bank tax evasion probe.
newsitem.headline: German prosecutors press bank tax evasion probe.

text.p: German prosecutors have found evidence of alleged tax evasion by 50 to 100 customers of Commerzbank AG in the Frankfurt region and expect to be able to uncover a further 1,000 similar cases at the bank nationwide, the Frankfurt state prosecutors' office said on Monday.

Job Tilmann, spokesman for the office, said about 200 Commerzbank customers had come forward to declare investments totalling 64 million marks in concealed accounts in Luxembourg, Gibraltar and Switzerland.
Tilmann said prosecutors were now investigating to what extent customers had evaded taxes on those investments.
Commerzbank could not immediately be reached for comment.
Prosecutors launched an investigation after they obtained a list containing account details of about 1,700 customers of Commerzbank's Luxembourg subsidiary Cisal in August 1995.
Clients are suspected of having evaded tax by failing to declare income from investments in tax havens like Luxembourg.

The investigation is part of a wider probe into German banks by tax authorities who have alleged bank staff abetted tax evasion by clients by helping them shift funds to hard-to-trace accounts abroad.

The probes, which have involved hundreds of raids on bank branches, followed the exodus of billions of marks to Luxembourg and other havens after Germany slapped a 30 percent withholding tax on interest income in 1994.
Moving funds abroad to avoid that tax is not illegal, but failing to report interest income to fiscal authorities in Germany is in breach of the law.

Senior German bank executives including Commerzbank chief executive Martin Kohlhaussen have complained vigorously that investigators were panicking customers who had opened accounts in Luxembourg in good faith and were also violating bank confidentiality codes.
